questions.question: Which of the following statements most accurately defines rule‑based reasoning and provides an appropriate example of its use?

options.A: It is a deductive process that generates new sentences by applying inference rules; e.g., using Modus Ponens on the Horn clauses C ∧ (B ⇒ A) to infer A.
options.B: It is a statistical method that estimates probabilities from data; e.g., learning a Markov Decision Process from STRIPS rules.
options.C: It is a neural‑network approach that adjusts weights through back‑propagation; e.g., training a deep model on image data.
options.D: It is a heuristic search that explores state spaces without formal inference; e.g., hill‑climbing on a SAT problem.

questions.explanation:
Rule‑based reasoning is the sound generation of new sentences from old using inference rules, exemplified by applying Modus Ponens on Horn clauses such as C ∧ (B ⇒ A) to derive A. (Context: forward/backward chaining, Horn clauses – pages 185‑186)

questions.question: Which scenario best illustrates forward chaining in a rule‑based deduction system?

options.A: Starting from the goal ‘A’, the system searches backward through Horn clauses until it finds premises that are known true.
options.B: Beginning with known facts {C, D}, the system repeatedly applies Horn‑clause rules to infer new facts until no more can be derived.
options.C: The system randomly selects literals to assign truth values and checks the whole knowledge base for consistency.
options.D: The system uses a Prolog query to match a rule head with a goal and then attempts to satisfy the body literals.

questions.explanation:
Forward chaining starts from known facts and iteratively applies Horn‑clause rules to infer additional facts, as described for Horn KBs on page 185.

---

questions.question: Given the Horn‑clause knowledge base KB = { P, Q ⇒ R, R ⇒ S }, which of the following conclusions can be derived by forward chaining?

options.A: S, because P and Q together allow R to be inferred, and then R yields S.
options.B: R, because P alone directly triggers the rule Q ⇒ R.
options.C: Q, because forward chaining can infer missing premises from conclusions.
options.D: None of the above, because forward chaining cannot operate on this KB.

questions.explanation:
Starting with fact P, forward chaining needs Q to fire Q ⇒ R; assuming Q is also known (or added), R is derived, then R ⇒ S gives S. This follows the forward‑chaining process for Horn clauses (page 185).

questions.question: In a Prolog program that uses the closed‑world assumption with the rule `alive(X) :- not dead(X).`, which of the following queries will succeed?

options.A: `alive(jane).` when the fact `dead(jane).` is present in the knowledge base.
options.B: `alive(jane).` when no fact about `dead(jane)` exists in the knowledge base.
options.C: `alive(jane).` only if `alive(jane).` is explicitly asserted as a fact.
options.D: `alive(jane).` will never succeed because Prolog cannot handle negation.

questions.explanation:
Under the closed‑world assumption, `not dead(jane)` succeeds when `dead(jane)` cannot be proven; thus `alive(jane)` succeeds if `dead(jane)` is absent. (Context: Prolog, closed‑world assumption – page 213)

questions.question: The truth‑table model‑checking function `TT‑CHECK‑ALL` has a time complexity of O(2ⁿ) for n symbols. What does this imply for the feasibility of exhaustive search as the number of symbols grows?

options.A: The runtime grows linearly, making exhaustive search practical for large n.
options.B: The runtime grows exponentially, quickly becoming infeasible as n increases.
options.C: The runtime is polynomial, so exhaustive search is efficient for any n.
options.D: The runtime is constant, independent of n.

questions.explanation: O(2ⁿ) denotes exponential growth in the number of symbols, meaning exhaustive truth‑table enumeration becomes rapidly impractical as n grows (page 184).
